caseStudies.name: Ruth George
caseStudies.summary: Ruth George, a 19-year-old University of Illinois Chicago student, was found dead in her car in a campus parking garage in November 2019. Prosecutors alleged that a man who tried to talk to her near a transit stop became angry when she ignored him, followed her into the garage and strangled her. A 26-year-old man was charged with first-degree murder and criminal sexual assault and held without bail. The outcome of the case could not be confirmed when this file was compiled.

caseStudies.name: Mary "Unique" Spears
caseStudies.summary: Mary Spears, a 27-year-old mother of three, was shot and killed in October 2014 at a hall in Detroit where her family had gathered after a funeral. Police and relatives said a man had approached her, she made clear she was not interested, and security escorted him out before he opened fire. Five other people were wounded. A 38-year-old man was charged with first-degree murder; the outcome of the case could not be confirmed when this file was compiled.

caseStudies.name: Janese Talton-Jackson
caseStudies.summary: Janese Talton-Jackson, 29, was shot and killed outside a bar in the Pittsburgh area in January 2016 after turning down a man's advances inside. The man pleaded guilty in February 2017 to third-degree murder and related charges and was sentenced to 20 to 40 years in prison. (Local reports also spell her name Ja-Nese Jackson Talton.)

caseStudies.name: Sarah Everard
caseStudies.summary: Sarah Everard, a 33-year-old marketing executive, was abducted in March 2021 while walking home from a friend's house in London. Prosecutors said a serving police officer staged a false arrest, using COVID-19 lockdown rules as a pretext. He was sentenced on 30 September 2021 to life in prison for her murder.

caseStudies.name: Sabina Nessa
caseStudies.summary: Sabina Nessa, a 28-year-old primary school teacher, was killed in September 2021 while making a short walk through a park near her home in south-east London to meet a friend. A man pleaded guilty to the attack and was sentenced in April 2022 to life in prison with a minimum term of 36 years.

caseStudies.name: Christina Yuna Lee
caseStudies.location: Chinatown, Manhattan, New York City, USA
caseStudies.summary: Christina Yuna Lee, 35, was killed inside her apartment in Manhattan's Chinatown on 13 February 2022. According to the Manhattan District Attorney, a man followed her into her building and up six flights of stairs as she arrived home at about 4:20 a.m. He pleaded guilty to murder and sexually motivated burglary and was sentenced in July 2024 to 30 years to life in prison.

caseStudies.name: Unnamed 18-year-old woman (2 train)
caseStudies.summary: On New Year's Day 2023, police said a man followed an 18-year-old woman onto a southbound 2 train in Manhattan and tried to sexually assault her as the train approached 72nd Street. Another passenger stepped in and helped her get to a different train car. She was taken to hospital for evaluation, and police later arrested a 23-year-old man.

caseStudies.name: Unnamed 20-year-old woman (Norwood Avenue station)
caseStudies.summary: In 2025 a man grabbed a 20-year-old woman on a J train platform at Norwood Avenue station in Brooklyn. Witnesses shouted at him to let her go, and police said at least five people held him until officers arrived. The woman had minor injuries, and a 42-year-old man was arrested and charged.

harasserBehaviour.finding: US national survey: 70% of harassed women said they had been harassed by one man acting alone, and 38% by two or more men (more than one answer allowed). Harassers of both women and men were overwhelmingly men.
US national survey: for sexual harassment (as opposed to assault) the most frequently named perpetrator was a stranger in person (42% of women who had experienced harassment or assault).

99 New York City incidents reported to Hollaback! (2005-2011): 79.8% included verbal harassment, 18.2% stalking, 14.1% lewd looks or staring, 11.1% assault, 10.1% flashing, 6.1% groping. Categories overlap. The sample is self-selected, so severe incidents are probably over-represented.

In the same 99 NYC incidents, the verbal content was most often an uninvited greeting (49.5%), followed by comments evaluating the woman's looks (31.3%), sexually suggestive remarks (26.3%) and explicitly sexual or violent language (14.1%).

In the same 99 NYC incidents: 60.6% happened on the street or sidewalk and 22.2% on or around the subway or bus; the woman was alone in about 78%; the harasser acted alone in about 76%; 34 incidents were described as daytime and 32 as night (33 gave no time), so night was not clearly more common; no incident involved a woman accompanied by one male companion.

Random sample of 223 NYC incidents submitted to Hollaback! (2005-2008): 57% included verbal interactions (mostly sexual comments, solicitations and threats), 29% physical touching and 12% groping or attempted groping; 55% happened in the street or a park and 16% on public transportation.

308 Hollaback! posts from New York and Chicago: 55.1% of harassers were on foot; in 42.9% the harasser used his body or a vehicle to affect the woman's movement (blocking her path, grabbing or following); 9.4% described the harasser making a quick exit afterwards; 38% took place at or near public transit.

546 incidents in 528 Hollaback London narratives (2012-2017): 68% verbal harassment, 28% physical contact (touching, groping, grabbing or assault) and 14% being followed or persistently stared at; 71% on the street and 17% on public transport; usually a lone woman and a lone man.

How women responded in the 546 London incidents: spoke or shouted at the harasser 40%; walked or ran away or hid 13%; said they did nothing 13% (most often no time, froze or scared); called on others at the time 7%; reported afterwards 6%; ignored 5%; physical response such as a push 5%; no response described 16%.

How women responded in the 99 NYC incidents: 41.4% tried to ignore the harasser or walked away; 39.4% verbally engaged him; 6 incidents involved physically defending herself and 6 were reported to police (the report prints 13.3% for these two, which does not match its own counts).

The London narratives describe every kind of outcome after a woman responds: men walking away, going quiet or even apologising; responses with no visible effect; and, rarely, escalation. The author describes violent retaliation as very rare in the sample and gives no rates.

Survey of 258 heterosexual men: about 33% reported catcalling behaviour in the past year. Their most common stated reasons were to show they like the woman (85%), to show sexual interest (83%) and because they see it as a normal way of flirting (73%). Only 7% endorsed punishing women and 6% wanting to make her self-conscious. The sample was mostly mild, infrequent catcallers.

The same catcallers mostly hoped for a friendly reaction: a smile (85%), flirting back (81%), a conversation (78%), feeling flattered (73%). A minority hoped she would be shocked (12%), intimidated (9%), angry (5%) or afraid (5%).
Men who reported catcalling scored higher than other men on hostile sexism, self-ascribed masculinity, social dominance orientation and tolerance of sexual harassment.

Two studies of US college men: men with a higher likelihood to sexually harass were more likely to report harassing strangers when in a group than alone, and group harassment was motivated by anonymity and group bonding.

Survey of 348 US undergraduates: men who believed they had less power than women were the most likely to report engaging in street harassment, and tolerance of sexual harassment was positively related to doing it.
A sociologist interviewed by PBS NewsHour describes street remarks as often intended to frighten or dominate, and as designed to go unnoticed by other people nearby.

Lab study with 77 men in a dating simulation: when a simulated date refused a sexual advance, 25 men (32%) gave an aggressive immediate response and 52 did not. Aggression was most likely among men high in sexual dominance motivation who formed very hostile views of the woman. This is a dating simulation with college men, not a street encounter.

Experiment on a mock dating platform: men, but not women, who were rejected by a desired partner showed increased hostility, both toward the person who rejected them and toward the opposite gender in general; anger explained the effect.
Experiment with 157 young men: after a romantic rejection, men whose sexual goals had been activated behaved more aggressively toward the woman who rejected them (measured by noise blasts).

Vignette studies summarised by Psychology Today: people who strongly endorse masculine honor beliefs expected a rejected man to feel insulted and less manly, rated aggressive reactions (such as grabbing her arm or insulting her) as more appropriate, and were less likely to expect him simply to walk away; a public rejection was seen as a bigger threat to his honor. Secondary summary; the original abstract could not be opened.

Two studies on excuses such as saying she already has a boyfriend: women who hold stronger masculine honor beliefs were more likely to use avoidant or deceptive rejections; men with stronger honor beliefs saw a deceptive rejection as a greater threat to the rejected man's honor; the authors suggest women use such excuses to soften the rejection and avoid retaliation. No data on how real harassers actually react.

US national survey (online dating context): 60% of women aged 18 to 34 who have used dating sites or apps say someone kept contacting them after they said they were not interested; 44% were called an offensive name and 19% were threatened with physical harm. These are lifetime experiences, not per-incident rates.
US national survey: about 22% of all women had been called a sexist slur such as 'bitch' or 'slut' by a stranger in public, and 25% had been the target of comments about their body or obscene sounds.

Focus groups: several women described a man reacting to being ignored with anger or insults (for example demanding to know why she was ignoring him and then calling her names), and one described a man parking his car and following her on foot after she ignored his offer of a ride. Qualitative accounts only; no rates.

Focus groups: one participant described a woman declining politely to give her number and the man turning belligerent anyway; another described a woman who finally said thank you to a persistent man, after which he backed off somewhat. Qualitative accounts only.

Focus groups: some women said that being pleasant, smiling or making small talk with men in public tends to lead to more approaches, so they act stern on purpose. This fits the finding that most catcallers hope for a smile or a conversation.

Focus groups: women described ending an episode of being followed by going into a shop (one lost a man who had followed her for about 45 minutes by leaving through a grocery store's back exit) and a venue's bouncer removing a harasser. The report recommends businesses act as safe havens. Anecdotal; no rates.

Practitioner guidance from Stop Street Harassment (drawing on self-defence and harassment experts): respond calmly and firmly, name the behaviour and say what you want, do not apologise or offer excuses, do not get drawn into his questions or guilt-tripping, repeat yourself or leave. It warns that swearing or losing your temper is the reaction most likely to be met with anger and violence. Expert guidance, not measured data.

Right To Be states there is no right or wrong way to respond because harassment is never the target's fault, that safety comes first, and that doing nothing, walking on or responding are all legitimate. Its founders report that years of confronting and trying to educate harassers did not seem to change them.

Cornell analysis of 223 NYC incidents: women who took some action, in the moment or afterwards, appeared to suffer less negative emotional impact. Those who responded assertively described outward-directed emotions such as anger; more passive responders described inward ones such as embarrassment, helplessness and fear.

Study of young adult women: stranger harassment was linked to self-objectification for women who used the common coping strategies (passive, self-blame or treating it as benign) but not for the few who used active coping such as confronting the harasser; harassment was also linked to fear of rape and to restricting one's movement.

In a 2014 hidden-camera video made for Hollaback!, a woman who walked silently through Manhattan for ten hours without responding was the target of more than 100 incidents of street harassment. It is a single edited case, so it shows only that staying silent does not prevent remarks.
The same 2014 video was criticised for over-representing men of colour in its editing, and the organisation apologised for the bias. Do not treat it as evidence about who harasses.
Most women cannot tell in the moment how an encounter will end: 68% of harassed women in the US national survey were concerned the incident would escalate.

A comprehensive review of 182 sources describes street harassment research as an emergent field with inconsistent definitions and typologies. The search behind this file found no study that measures how harassers react to specific responses from the person targeted.

fiveDs.name: Distract
fiveDs.description: An indirect, low-key way to interrupt the incident: ignore the person doing the harassing, engage the person being harassed, and talk about something unrelated.
fiveDs.example: Ask her for directions or the time, or greet her as if she were a friend you have just bumped into, and stand between the two of them.

fiveDs.name: Delegate
fiveDs.description: Ask someone else to help: the person next to you or someone with authority in the space. Say clearly what you see and what you want them to do.
fiveDs.example: Tell a shop worker, bus driver or station agent what is happening and ask them to step in. Do not call the police unless the person being harassed asks you to.

fiveDs.name: Document
fiveDs.description: Record or take notes on what is happening, but only if someone else is already helping and you are safe.
fiveDs.example: Film from a safe distance, then give the footage to the person who was harassed and let them decide what happens to it. Never post it without their permission.

fiveDs.name: Delay
fiveDs.description: If you cannot act in the moment, check in with the person afterwards; it reduces the harm even when the incident is over.
fiveDs.example: Ask whether she is okay, tell her you saw it and it was not acceptable, and offer to walk with her or sit with her for a while.

fiveDs.name: Direct
fiveDs.description: Name the behaviour or tell the person to stop, briefly and firmly. Use with caution: it is the riskiest option because the person may turn on you or escalate.
fiveDs.example: Say one short, calm sentence telling him to leave her alone, then turn your attention to her. Do not argue or debate.

findings.finding: Right To Be's 5Ds are Distract, Delegate, Document, Delay and Direct. Distract, Delegate and Direct came from the Green Dot programme (2012 partnership); Delay was added in 2015 and Document in 2017. Four of the five are indirect and are designed not to escalate.
Across eight countries, only 25% of people who experienced sexual harassment in public spaces said someone helped them.
Across the same eight countries, 86% of people said they did not know what to do when they witnessed sexual harassment in public.
In 223 New York City incidents, bystanders were present in 31%. Where present, they had a positive effect 26% of the time, a negative effect 22% of the time and took no action 19% of the time.
In the same NYC sample, harassment was more likely to stop when a bystander confronted the harasser. The report gives no percentage.
Help did not have to be dramatic: a knowing look or a supportive, empathetic remark was enough to improve how the targeted woman felt.
When bystanders were present but did nothing, their presence tended to make the target's negative feelings worse, and writers described that inaction as unacceptable.
In the US national survey, 20% of women and 23% of men said they had spoken up or done something to help someone else who was being harassed.

In a Swiss survey (4,035 valid responses, not representative), 68% had witnessed street harassment; 45% of those witnesses had never intervened, mainly because they did not know what to do. The most common intervention was speaking to the harasser (about 30%), then supporting the target (about 20%).

A meta-analysis of more than 7,700 participants and 105 effect sizes confirms the classic bystander effect (individuals are less likely to help when others are present; overall effect g = -0.35), but the effect is weaker when the situation is clearly dangerous, when a perpetrator is present, and when bystanders know each other.

In 219 real public conflicts filmed by street cameras in the UK, the Netherlands and South Africa, at least one bystander did something to help in 9 out of 10 cases, and more bystanders meant a higher chance that someone would act. The study covers public aggression generally, not sexual harassment.

Right To Be advises using Direct with caution because the person harassing may turn on the bystander or escalate. Before speaking up, check four things: you are physically safe, the person being harassed is physically safe, escalation seems unlikely, and the person seems to want someone to speak up. Keep it short and do not argue.

A real example of the risk: in November 2022 a 54-year-old subway rider in the Bronx who stepped in to defend a woman who was being harassed was stabbed in the elbow; a suspect was arrested at the scene.
Right To Be advises against calling the police on someone's behalf unless that person has asked for it, because some people do not feel safe with police involvement.
Right To Be advises documenting only when someone else is already helping, and always letting the person who was harassed decide what happens to the recording.
Among 99 New York City incidents, none happened while the woman was accompanied by a man,. This is consistent with Distract tactics in which a bystander simply joins the woman.

modelCalibration.notes: How to read this table. basis=data means the value is taken directly from a cited figure (the range shows the spread across sources; a single-source figure has a point range). basis=inferred means the value was derived from cited figures collected in a different setting or by combining figures. basis=assumption means no measurement exists and the value is a conservative placeholder; where the rationale says the direction or ordering is evidence-based, only the ordering should be treated as supported. Key limits: (1) No study measures how street harassers react to specific responses, so every response.* and bystander.<tactic>.* value is an assumption except where marked. (2) Incident-type shares come from self-selected story archives (Hollaback!) that over-represent memorable and severe incidents; national surveys give lifetime prevalence, not per-encounter rates. (3) Rejection-aggression experiments involve college men in dating or lab settings, not strangers on a street. Design guidance that follows from the evidence: let most of the variance come from the man's disposition, which is drawn at the start of a run, and let the trainee's response shift probabilities only modestly; never make a bad outcome the scripted consequence of a particular choice, because the evidence does not support a 'correct' response and guidance is explicit that harassment is not the target's fault; keep physical escalation rare; make friendly engagement prolong contact, insults the most likely to draw hostility, and reaching other people or a shop the most reliable way to end the encounter; in the bystander part, make indirect tactics low-risk and Direct effective but riskier for the bystander.

parameters.rationale: Share of reported incidents that include verbal harassment: 79.8% (99 NYC incidents), 68% (546 London incidents), 57% (223 NYC incidents).
Share of reported incidents involving stalking or following: 18.2% (NYC, n=99); 14% followed or persistently stared at (London). Lifetime prevalence among US women is 20% (2014) to 34% (2018).

42.9% of 308 New York and Chicago Hollaback! posts described the harasser using his body or a vehicle to affect the woman's movement (blocking, grabbing or following). Self-selected posts, so treat as an upper bound for everyday encounters.

Share of reported incidents with physical contact: 6.1% groping and 11.1% assault (NYC, n=99); 12% groping or attempted groping and 29% any physical touching (NYC, n=223); 28% (London). These archives over-represent severe incidents.

No source reports this directly. Reported-incident archives put physical contact at 6-29% and following at 14-18% with unknown overlap, which implies roughly 55-70% non-contact, non-following incidents; archives over-sample severe incidents and far more US women report verbal harassment (57%) than touching (23%) or following (20%), so the everyday rate is probably higher.

No per-encounter denominator exists anywhere. Set deliberately below the 6-12% groping or assault share seen in self-selected incident archives. Physical escalation should stay rare and must never be scripted as the consequence of a particular trainee choice.
70% of harassed US women were harassed by one man (national survey); about 76% of NYC incidents involved a lone perpetrator.
55.1% of harassers in 308 New York and Chicago posts were on foot.
About 78% of 99 NYC incidents happened when the woman was alone.
Bystanders were present in 31% of 223 NYC incidents.
25% of people harassed in public say someone helped (eight-country Ipsos survey); bystanders had a positive effect in 26% of NYC incidents where they were present.
86% of people say they do not know what to do when they witness harassment (Ipsos); in a Swiss survey 45% of witnesses had never intervened, mainly for that reason.

About 1 in 10 US women who experienced harassment or assault filed an official report; 4% (NYC subway survey), 12% (NYC transit survey), 6% (London narratives) and 6 of 99 NYC incidents were reported.
68% of harassed US women were very or somewhat concerned the incident would escalate (25% very concerned). Useful for pacing the trainee's sense of uncertainty rather than the man's behaviour.
Among self-reported catcallers, 85% hoped for a smile, 81% for flirting back, 78% for a conversation and 73% that she would feel flattered. The sample was mostly mild, infrequent catcallers.

Among self-reported catcallers, 5% hoped for fear or anger, 9% hoped she would feel intimidated, 12% shocked, and 7% endorsed punishing women. The surveyed men were at the mild end, so the true share among persistent night-time harassers may be higher.

No data on the share of harassers who keep going after a clear no. Guided loosely by the finding that catcallers score higher on hostile sexism and tolerance of harassment, and by online-dating data showing that persistence after a refusal is a common experience for young women.
In a lab dating simulation, 25 of 77 men (32%) reacted aggressively to a clear sexual refusal. Different setting (college men, simulated date), so applied with a wide range.

No rates exist. Narrative studies describe men walking away, going quiet or apologising after women spoke back, alongside cases with no effect; practitioner guidance recommends a short, calm, firm statement.
No rates exist. Focus-group accounts show ignoring sometimes triggers anger and insults, but there is no evidence on how often, or on whether it is more or less common than after an explicit refusal.

No rates exist. A woman who stayed silent for ten hours in Manhattan still drew over 100 remarks, and focus-group accounts describe men following after being ignored. The scenario's man is persistent by design, so this is set higher than the 14-18% following rate in incident archives.
No rates exist. Ignoring or walking away was the most common response in NYC reports (41%), most reported incidents are verbal only, and Right To Be notes that much harassment happens in passing.

No rates exist. Guidance says apologies and excuses invite negotiation, and most catcallers are hoping for conversation, so a soft answer is assumed to prolong the exchange more often than a firm one.

No rates exist. Focus-group accounts include a polite refusal met with belligerence, so this cannot be zero; set below the firm-boundary value because a soft refusal poses less of a public status threat.

Magnitude is a guess; the ordering is evidence-based. Practitioner guidance identifies swearing or losing one's temper as the reaction most likely to provoke anger and violence, and honor-belief research links perceived insult to endorsement of aggression. Keep this the highest hostility value.
No rates exist. Narrative research describes violent retaliation as very rare; this covers stepping closer, threats or blocking rather than physical contact.
No rates exist. Research on the boyfriend excuse measures perceptions, not harasser behaviour; guidance warns that excuses invite argument (for example questioning the excuse).
No rates exist. Women report using excuses to soften rejection and avoid retaliation, and men with strong honor beliefs see deception as an added honor threat if detected.
No rates exist. Guidance notes that visibly recording details can scare a harasser into stopping and that harassers rely on going unnoticed; group-harassment research points to anonymity as a motive.
No rates exist. A public threat is a status challenge, so hostility is assumed to be somewhat more likely than after ignoring and less likely than after an insult.
No rates exist. Focus-group accounts describe shops and venue staff ending episodes of following, and harassers overwhelmingly target women who are alone (78% of NYC incidents).
Magnitude is a guess; the direction is evidence-based. Most catcallers hope for a smile or conversation, and women in focus groups report that being pleasant leads to more approaches.

Magnitude is a guess; the direction is evidence-based. The NYC analysis found harassment was more likely to stop when a bystander confronted the harasser but gives no number, and no reported NYC incident involved a woman accompanied by a man.
No outcome data by tactic. Joining the woman removes the condition under which most incidents occur (woman alone) without challenging the man.
No outcome data. Right To Be describes Distract as an option when open confrontation might escalate.
Magnitude is a guess; the direction is evidence-based. Confrontation by a bystander made harassment more likely to stop in NYC incidents (no number given).
No rates exist. Right To Be warns Direct can redirect abuse to the bystander or escalate, and real cases of bystanders being injured exist. Should be clearly higher than for Distract.
No outcome data. Depends on whether the delegate (shop worker, transit staff, another passer-by) acts; group presence increases the chance that someone intervenes.
No outcome data. Right To Be says documenting alone, while nobody is helping, can add to the target's distress; its value is mainly after the fact.

Magnitude is a guess; the direction is evidence-based. Even a supportive look or remark improved how targets felt, and Right To Be says checking in afterwards reduces harm. Delay does not change the harasser's behaviour.
Magnitude is a guess; the direction is evidence-based. Bystanders who were present and did nothing made targets feel worse.

Flag, not a probability: in real public conflicts, more bystanders present meant a higher chance that at least one intervened, and at least one helped in about 9 of 10 conflicts. The classic bystander effect (each individual less likely to act) is weaker when danger is clear and a perpetrator is present.
